headlines.title: Pedestrian struck, killed by vehicle in SF's Richmond District
headlines.description: A pedestrian died after being struck by a motorist in San Francisco’s Richmond District on Monday afternoon, according to police. The collision was reported at 2:08 p.m. at the intersection of Arguello Boulevard and Anza Street. The pedestrian was taken to a hospital but died there, San Francisco police said. The driver of the vehicle involved in the collision stayed at the scene and cooperated with investigators, according to police. The name of the pedestrian was not immediately available.

headlines.title: OpenAI kicks off Developer Day in San Francisco
headlines.description: OpenAI kicked off its annual Developer Day on Monday with the company announcing a slew of new artificial intelligence products. The conference is being held at San Francisco’s Fort Mason and comes as OpenAI is under scrutiny for a string of incident where its AI has gone rogue. OpenAI has paused development of some models after reviewing incidents where its agents hacked other companies, as well as a healthcare website for the Australian government. In addition, OpenAI on Monday said it was delaying the release of a new artificial intelligence model out of security concerns voiced by its researchers, the latest in the company’s effort to decelerate the pace of the technology’s advance. Artificial intelligence Sep 26 Artificial intelligence Sep 22 Artificial intelligence Sep 17 OpenAI’s decision to hold back the model, called GPT-6.1 Astra, comes amid a broader push within the industry to slow the development of increasingly autonomous systems until safety measures can catch up. The announcement also came before AI executives were set to huddle with President Donald Trump in Washington as technology companies face new pressure to be accountable for how their models can be abused. Recent surveys show Americans have growing concerns about AI. Protesters outside the Developer Day conference also raised issues about AI use by federal agents like the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has joined other industry leaders in calling for a slowdown, warning that companies do not yet have adequate safeguards to control the most capable systems. Altman delivered the keynote address for the Developer Day conference, while OpenAI President Greg Brockman was expected to attend the White House’s event Tuesday.
headlines.source: Thomas Beaumont | Associated Press and NBC Bay Area staff

headlines.title: 5 hurt in multi-vehicle crash in East Palo Alto
headlines.description: Five people were injured in a multi-vehicle crash in East Palo Alto Tuesday morning, according to the San Mateo County Sheriff’s Office. The crash happened at about 8:20 a.m. in the area of Bay Road and University Avenue, the sheriff’s office said. Of the five people who were injured, two adults suffered life-threatening injuries, according to the sheriff’s office. The conditions of the three other people weren’t immediately known. The cause of the crash is under investigation.

headlines.title: San Jose leaders to vote on parking meter rate increase
headlines.description: The cost to park in downtown San Jose could soon be going up. The San Jose City Council on Tuesday is scheduled to vote on a plan to double the downtown parking meter rate to $4 per hour and extend parking meter hours to 9 p.m. instead of the current end time of 6 p.m. One member of the city’s Downtown Parking Board sent an open letter to the council recommending it postpone the vote. Tuesday’s meeting starts at 1:30 p.m.

headlines.title: New California law bans officers from using gloves that deliver electric shocks
headlines.description: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a law Tuesday banning local, state and federal law enforcement officers from using gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks to people. The ban on shock gloves will take effect next year and remain in place until 2030. It comes weeks after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement moved to equip its officers with the gloves, which are designed to gain compliance from combative individuals. Last month, the agency awarded a nearly $17 million contract to buy 6,000 pairs. “Trump has put his political interests above the health, safety and livelihood of American families,” Newsom said in a statement. “California is taking action to strengthen transparency, accountability, and oversight around immigration enforcement in our state.” The law is the latest example of how Democratic-led states have been pushing back against President Donald Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts since he took office last year. In California, lawmakers passed at least two dozen bills this year seeking to fortify immigrants’ rights, restrict cooperation with federal immigration agents and tighten regulations on immigrant detention facilities, among other things. Nationwide, 17 states with Democratic-led legislatures have passed a total of more than 100 pro-immigrant bills this year, according to an Associated Press analysis using the bill tracking software Plural. The most common purpose is to limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement agents. Democratic California Assemblymember LaShae Sharp-Collins said she introduced the shock-gloves legislation to “put a pause” on law enforcement’s use of the devices while the state examines their potential risks. The law requires the state’s Justice Department to study their safety and report to lawmakers by 2029. “There’s a lot of unrest and a lot of uncertainty,” she said in an interview. “A lot of people are scared.” The law will again test the state’s authority to restrict federal agents amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. A federal judge earlier this year blocked the state’s first-in-the-nation law barring federal officers from wearing face coverings, deeming it too selective because it applied to local and federal law enforcement but exempted state officers. Lawmakers passed a new bill this year to make the ban apply to all officers. Newsom signed that legislation. Kevin Johnson, a professor emeritus at the University of California, Davis, School of Law, said courts are likely to ultimately rule that the state cannot bar federal officers from wearing shock gloves or face coverings. The laws are well-intentioned, he said, but likely conflict with the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution, which generally sets federal law as supreme over conflicting state law. “The state has very limited, if any, powers in dictating to the federal government how its officers are armed,” he said. California law enforcement groups broadly opposed the ban. Sacramento Sheriff Jim Cooper, a Democrat and former state lawmaker, said banning shock gloves “really makes no sense” because they are among the non-lethal tools officers can use if necessary. “When the federal government does something, the state Legislature wants to ban it,” he said at a news conference. “They’re making our job harder.” Sharp-Collins said ICE’s plan to use shock gloves was the catalyst for the ban. But she cited their use by other officers, including a case in which a Kentucky family alleges a man died after being tased and shocked with the gloves dozens of times while in law enforcement custody in 2024. State Sen. Scott Wiener, a San Francisco Democrat who wrote last year’s mask ban, also authored this year’s measure to expand it to state officers. “California must use every available tool to stand up for our communities under attack from ICE’s secret police terror campaign,” he said in a statement after it passed the Legislature. ___ Associated Press writer David A. Lieb contributed to this report from Jefferson City, Missouri.

headlines.title: San Francisco to keep Flock cameras with new limits on data access
headlines.description: San Francisco will keep its Flock license plate cameras but put new limits on who can access the data they record, Mayor Daniel Lurie announced Tuesday. Under the new policy, officers will need approval from leadership and a connection to an active criminal investigation to search license plate data. The data will also be removed from Flock’s platform after 30 days. San Francisco police will keep their own copy for up to a year. Lurie said the cameras help police solve crimes as concerns grow about how the data could be misused. Assemblymember Matt Haney also plans to introduce a state bill that would make it a crime for officers to improperly share license plate data. The bill is expected sometime in December.

headlines.title: Preliminary 2.6 magnitude earthquake strikes near Yountville
headlines.description: A preliminary 2.6 magnitude earthquake struck near Yountville Tuesday morning, according to the United States Geological Survey. The quake hit at 9:06 a.m. and was centered 2.9 miles south-southwest of Oakville, 7.6 miles north-northeast of Sonoma and 10.3 miles northwest of Napa, the USGS said. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates. headlines.title: Bicyclist, electric scooter rider injured in separate San Jose collisions
headlines.description: A bicyclist and an electric scooter rider were injured Monday in separate collisions in San Jose, according to police. The first collision happened at about 3:05 p.m. near the intersection of South Seventh and East Virginia streets, police said. A bicyclist was taken to a local hospital to be treated for non-life-threatening injuries, according to police. The driver stayed at the scene and cooperated with investigators. The second collision happened at roughly 6:09 p.m. in the area of McKee Road and Interstate 680, police said. A man riding an electric scooter was taken to local hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, according to police. The driver remained at the scene and was cooperative with the investigation. Alcohol and/or drugs do not appear to have played a role in either collision, police said. Both collisions are under investigation.

headlines.title: Pedestrian, driver killed in 2 separate collisions in Sonoma County
headlines.description: Two people died Monday night in Sonoma County in separate traffic collisions, the California Highway Patrol said. The first collision was reported at 8:40 p.m. on State Route 116 by Sparkes Road south of Sebastopol. According to the CHP, a pedestrian attempted to cross the road in the dark and was fatally struck by an oncoming vehicle. State Route 116 was closed for the investigation and the CHP estimated it would be reopened at about 2:30 a.m. Tuesday. The second collision was reported at 9:13 p.m. at 690 Tomales Road in a rural area of the county west of Petaluma. According to the CHP, a solo vehicle crash occurred and the vehicle went off the roadway, caught fire and then started a grass fire. The driver died. The CHP will release more information about these fatal collisions on Tuesday, Officer David Derutte said.

headlines.title: 16-year-old boy shot, injured at weekend house party in Antioch
headlines.description: A teenage boy was shot and injured this weekend at a party in Antioch, police said Monday. On Saturday just before 9 p.m., multiple calls began to come in reporting gunshots in the 5400 block of Prewett Ranch Drive, according to police. While officers were responding to the area, dispatch received a report that a 16-year-old boy from Brentwood had been dropped off at a local hospital with a gunshot wound. The victim told police he was leaving a house party on Prewett Ranch Drive when the shooting occurred. The boy was treated for his gunshot wound to the abdomen and is expected to survive. Officers processing the scene on Prewett Ranch Drive confirmed the shooting was connected to the nearby house party, the department said. Detectives also discovered that two nearby residences had been struck by gunfire. No additional injuries were reported. Police are actively investigating the case and are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the shooting, the department said, but so far, no suspect has been identified. Anyone with information about this shooting, or anyone who has home surveillance or dashcam footage from the area around the time of the crime, is encouraged to contact the Antioch Police Department at 925-778-2441.

headlines.title: Federal judge to decide future of oversight for Oakland Police Department
headlines.description: A federal judge is expected to decide Tuesday whether more than two decades of federal oversight of the Oakland Police Department will come to an end. There are a couple of possible outcomes. Federal oversight could end altogether, leaving Oakland to run its own police department, or the department could remain under federal court oversight. Ending federal oversight has been supported by the city of Oakland and civil rights advocates. Last weekend, a coalition called Safe Oakland gathered to say it is time for the community to take over and for the city to run its own department. It has been more than two decades since the city of Oakland settled a class-action police abuse lawsuit involving 119 people for $11 million. Four officers were prosecuted on felony misconduct charges stemming from the so-called “Oakland Riders” scandal, but none were convicted. The scandal led to a court-approved agreement requiring sweeping reforms. Earlier this year, a federal judge declared the department in compliance with all reform measures. More recently, OPD’s federal monitor reported the department had fallen short of compliance with a specific benchmark requiring timely investigations of officer misconduct complaints. Two civil rights attorneys are proposing a one-year extension of oversight by a federal judge. A federal court hearing is expected later Tuesday. Oakland Sep 23 Oakland May 27 Oakland Jun 1, 2022

headlines.title: Woman accused of hate crimes in viral San Jose video appears in court
headlines.description: The woman at the center of a viral video in which she is accused of making discriminatory remarks to a father and his child was back in court Tuesday. Lindsay Hansen smiled as an NBC Bay Area crew took photos of her during her appearance at the Hall of Justice. Hansen was arrested on charges that include stalking and hate crimes after she allegedly approached the father and child while in her vehicle earlier this month. Police say she is also responsible for other incidents in San Jose, including one at a high school. Hansen’s court appearance Tuesday was continued. She is due back in court Thursday morning.
